proposal: The Mandate recommends defining irregular warfare broadly in the National Security Strategy, characterizing irregular threats there by region, building irregular warfare into the National Defense Strategy with USSOCOM named as lead, and establishing an Irregular Warfare Center of Excellence. It also recommends USSOCOM-led regional operations and information operations to counter China's Belt and Road Initiative, directly countering Chinese economic power in North America, Central America and the Caribbean, a name-and-shame approach toward entities that target democratic processes, economic warfare and lawfare against hostile actors, and keeping aggressive counterterrorism authorities. The offensive cyber item on the same page is tracked in c04-21.

status_summary: The National Security Strategy, released 2025-12-04 with a cover dated November 2025, does not use the terms irregular warfare, Belt and Road, special operations or lawfare, but its Western Hemisphere section says the United States will deny non-hemispheric competitors control of strategically vital assets, press partners to wind down foreign control of ports and key infrastructure and warn of the hidden costs of low-cost foreign assistance. The record for the 2026 National Defense Strategy (c04-08) found no use of the phrase irregular warfare there. The Irregular Warfare Center already existed in statute (10 U.S.C. 345, subsection added by Public Law 117-263 Sec. 1204 in December 2022); Public Law 119-60 Sec. 1204 (2025-12-18) made the Assistant Secretary of Defense for Special Operations and Low-Intensity Conflict its Executive Agent in place of the Director of the Defense Security Cooperation Agency, and the same law lists a Sec. 1094 on an Irregular Warfare Exercise Laboratory whose text was not read. No USSOCOM tasking against the Belt and Road Initiative or lead designation for irregular warfare was found.

timeline.event: The White House released the 2025 National Security Strategy, which does not use the term irregular warfare and, in its Western Hemisphere section, commits to denying non-hemispheric competitors control of strategic assets such as ports and key infrastructure.

The FY2026 NDAA (Public Law 119-60) was signed; its table of contents lists Sec. 1094 (Irregular Warfare Exercise Laboratory) and Sec. 1204 (modification to the Irregular Warfare Center and Regional Defense Fellowship Program).

title: Make irregular warfare a strategy cornerstone with a SOCOM lead and China BRI counters
uncertainties: The National Security Strategy text was read in summarized form, not word by word, by the researcher and again in this review; the absence of terms rests on that summarized reading. The release date of 2025-12-04 comes from the Council on Foreign Relations and a law firm summary; the White House PDF has a November 2025 cover and a December 2025 upload path. The National Defense Strategy was not read directly; its omission of the phrase irregular warfare relies on record c04-08. The Sec. 1204 effect is taken from the U.S. Code amendment note on law.cornell.edu, which is partly primary and was re-read in review; the govinfo.gov HTML and XML of Public Law 119-60 and S. 1071 are cut short before Titles X and XII, so neither section body was read there, and the Sec. 1094 body is unread. congress.gov could not be opened in this review. A Federal Register API query for irregular warfare since 2025-01-20 (run in review on 2026-10-18) returned one unrelated presidential document on the Alien Enemies Act. The Western Hemisphere language is a strategy statement, which counts at most as proposed. A DOD News item of 2025-04-09 shows SOCOM leaders describing irregular warfare as department-wide, which is context, not a tracked action. The counterterrorism-authorities item was not tested separately. A statutory Center that predates 2025-01-20 is not evidence of a new action beyond the Executive Agent change.
